title: Databases
description: The components of a database management system, how relational databases organize data, how locks and ACID maintain data integrity, and SQL injection.

nodes.title: Components of a Database Management System (DBMS)
nodes.description:
A database stores an organized collection of structured data in tables with rows and columns, which makes the data easy to add, access, modify and analyze.
Relational databases, the focus of this map, relate data in one table to data in other tables, based on a relational model.
A DBMS is the collection of components that let people and processes control and use the database.

children.title: Hardware
children.description: The first component. The DBMS runs on a server that must provide enough processing power and storage space.

children.title: Software
children.description:
An operating system, and the DBMS software that runs on it.
Examples of DBMSs: MySQL, Oracle RDBMS, IBM DB2, Microsoft SQL Server, Amazon RDS and many others.

children.title: Database
children.description:
The DBMS software controls the database.
A database contains one or more tables.

children.title: Tables
children.description: Tables contain rows and columns of data.

children.title: Rows = Tuples / Records
children.description: The horizontal entries of a table. Each one holds all the data for one item, such as one student.

children.title: Columns = Attributes
children.description: The vertical divisions of a table. Each one holds one kind of data for every item, such as a student's last name.

children.title: Fields
children.description: The intersection of a tuple (row) and an attribute (column): one cell of data in the table.

children.title: Primary & Foreign Keys
children.description:
How a relational database relates data in one table to data in another table.
- The first kind: a unique identifier for a specific record (row). For a person, it could be a social insurance number, a passport number or a student ID.
- The second kind: a column whose values match the unique identifiers in another table. It forms the link, the relationship, to that table.
Example: a course registration table has a row for each course a student is registered in, and each row holds the student ID, which points to that student's row in the students table. The student ID links students to the courses they are registered in.

children.title: Language (SQL)
children.description:
The standard _____ users and processes use to communicate with and control a relational DBMS: to query, insert, update and delete data.
Full name: Structured Query Language.

children.title: Users
children.description: Users or processes send SQL commands to the DBMS to store new data, modify data, delete data and so on.

children.title: Data
children.description: The final major component: all the data stored in the DBMS.

nodes.title: Maintaining Integrity of Data
nodes.description:
A database is of little use to an organization if its data is inaccurate.
Controls such as locks and the ACID properties keep the data accurate and trustworthy, especially when many transactions run at the same time.

children.title: Concurrency
children.description:
Modern high-performance databases usually run many transactions at the same time, in parallel.
A transaction is a unit of work, usually several operations such as reads, writes and acquiring locks.
When many users or processes run transactions at once, maintaining data integrity is much harder.

children.title: Locks
children.description:
A major control to prevent data corruption when many transactions run at the same time.
While one transaction holds a record (tuple), only that user or process can update it, until it is released by committing the update or rolling back.

children.title: A - Atomicity
children.description:
ACID is a standard set of properties that guarantee database transactions are processed reliably. Enforce them to further protect data integrity.
This property: a transaction is all or nothing. All its changes take effect, or none do.

children.title: C - Consistency
children.description: Every transaction moves the database from one valid state to another: updates must obey the database's rules, such as constraints. The rules are enforced.

children.title: I - Isolation
children.description: Transactions running at the same time do not interfere with each other: a transaction's changes are invisible to other users until it is complete.

children.title: D - Durability
children.description: Once a transaction is committed, its changes are permanent and survive system failures such as a crash or power loss.

nodes.title: SQL Injection
nodes.description:
A major attack against databases. You definitely need to understand it for the exam.
An attacker sends malicious database commands through a web application's input fields to control the database behind it. Security professionals should always work to prevent it, mainly with input validation.
Covered in detail in the Domain 3 vulnerabilities mind map.
